rows.title: NHS legitimacy is increasingly an access-time problem: care quality remains more trusted than the ability to reach it
rows.source_unit: National Centre for Social Research, British Social Attitudes 43, Waiting for treatment
rows.geography: Great Britain; BSA adult respondents, with service-performance comparisons primarily for England and historical NHS series

observations.period: 1983-2025; overall NHS satisfaction and dissatisfaction

denominator.unit: unweighted BSA respondents in the 2025 overall NHS satisfaction series; historical bases vary

satisfied_1997.unit: percent very or quite satisfied with the NHS

legitimacy_route.value: Public satisfaction can recover over years when system performance becomes visibly better, but post-pandemic legitimacy remains historically weak

observations.period: 2023-2025; waiting as the dominant dissatisfaction route

denominator.unit: unweighted BSA respondents in the 2025 overall satisfaction series; service-specific item bases vary

waiting_dissatisfaction_2023.unit: percent citing long waits for a GP or hospital appointment as a reason for NHS dissatisfaction

hospital_appointment_time_satisfaction.unit: percent satisfied with the time before a hospital appointment in the latest survey

ae_wait_satisfaction.unit: percent satisfied with time spent waiting in A&E

gp_wait_satisfaction.unit: percent satisfied with GP appointment waiting time

waiting_as_hidden_price.value: Access time is experienced as a system cost and a visible test of whether public provision is reachable

observations.period: 2010-2025; quality and access diverge across NHS services

denominator.unit: unweighted BSA respondents in the 2025 specific-service satisfaction comparison; item bases and service availability vary

care_quality_satisfied.unit: percent satisfied with quality of care provided by the NHS in the latest comparison

hospital_appointment_satisfied.unit: percent satisfied with time before hospital appointment

ae_satisfaction_2010.unit: percent satisfied with accident and emergency

ae_satisfaction_latest.unit: percent satisfied with accident and emergency

quality_access_split.value: The public can remain more positive about care quality than about the time and route required to reach care

observations.period: 1997-2010 versus 2024-2025; resources, productivity, and visible feedback

denominator.unit: Historical BSA survey, NHS performance, workforce, demographic, and fiscal indicators combined in a comparative chapter; no single respondent denominator

waiting_list_pandemic_change.unit: percent increase in the number waiting for treatment at end-2021 compared with 2020

ae_four_hour_2002_03.unit: percent leaving A&E within four hours in 2002/03

ae_four_hour_2010.unit: percent leaving A&E within four hours by the end of New Labour

ae_four_hour_2024.unit: percent leaving A&E within four hours when Labour regained office

policy_feedback.value: Funding, targets, staffing, choice, migration, social care, and productivity are linked to legitimacy only when they become visible as shorter waits and reachable service

rows.title: Diary-based time use shows care and disability as hidden conversion costs for free time and social life
rows.source_unit: Australian Bureau of Statistics, How Australians use their time, 2024; supplementary disability, carer, and time-pressure tables released August 5, 2026
rows.geography: Australia; people aged 15 years and over in in-scope private households

observations.period: 2024 Time Use Survey; two diary days per in-scope person; total population averages

denominator.unit: assigned diary days per person for the main survey design; the published tables provide weighted national estimates

free_time_participation.unit: percent participating in free-time activities on a diary day

in_person_socialising_participation.unit: percent talking and socialising in person on a diary day

free_time_average_total_population.unit: hours:minutes average per day across the total population

in_person_socialising_average_total_popu.unit: hours:minutes average per day among people who participated in the activity

observations.period: 2024 Time Use Survey; disability-status supplementary tables

denominator.unit: weighted national population frame for people aged 15 years and over, split by ABS disability status; table reports participation and participant-time averages

in_person_socialising_participation_has_.unit: percent of people with disability participating on a diary day

in_person_socialising_participation_no_d.unit: percent of people without disability participating on a diary day

free_time_average_among_participants_has.unit: hours:minutes average per day among people with disability who participated in free time

free_time_average_among_participants_no_.unit: hours:minutes average per day among people without disability who participated in free time

mechanism.value: Disability does not appear as a simple attendance gap in the diary-day socialising measure, but participant time differs: access, energy, health, transport, and available alternatives may shape the duration and composition of free time after participation occurs

observations.period: 2024 Time Use Survey; carer-status supplementary tables

denominator.unit: weighted national population frame for people aged 15 years and over, split by whether the person reported providing care to another person

caring_support_participation_carers.unit: percent of people who provided care to another person participating in caring and support on a diary day

caring_support_participation_noncarers.unit: percent of people who did not provide care to another person participating in caring and support on a diary day

caring_support_average_among_participant.unit: hours:minutes average per day among carers who participated in caring and support
hours:minutes average per day among non-carers who participated in caring and support

free_time_average_among_participants_car.unit: hours:minutes average per day among carers who participated in free time

free_time_average_among_participants_non.unit: hours:minutes average per day among non-carers who participated in free time

mechanism.value: Care is a hidden time-price route: carers are much more likely to record caring and support on the diary day and spend longer in that activity, while their participant-level free-time average is slightly lower

rows.title: Unpaid care is becoming an employment-continuity fault line: workers cut hours, absorb stress, or leave depending on the support around them
rows.source_unit: Carers UK, Balancing work and unpaid care: a critical issue
rows.geography: United Kingdom; adults and workers with current or past unpaid-care experience

observations.period: July 14-17, 2026; current unpaid care and comparison with 2019

denominator.unit: UK adults; item-specific worker and carer bases vary

workers_combining_paid_and_unpaid_care.unit: percent of UK workers, estimated 6.7 million

workers_combining_paid_and_unpaid_care_2.unit: percent of UK workers, estimated 4.9 million in the comparable 2019 survey

current_unpaid_care.unit: percent of UK adults, estimated 11 million

current_unpaid_care_2019.unit: percent of UK adults, estimated 8.8 million in the comparable 2019 survey

scale_mechanism.value: Unpaid care is increasingly present inside working life, making employment continuity a care-system outcome as well as an individual choice.

observations.period: July 14-17, 2026; employment adaptations associated with unpaid care

denominator.unit: UK adults; item-specific bases vary

reduced_hours.unit: percent of UK adults, estimated 4.1 million, reporting reduced hours because of caring; about 20% among current carers

left_work_at_some_point.unit: percent of UK adults, estimated 3.3 million, reporting giving up work to care; 16% among current carers

left_work_last_two_years.unit: estimated people who left work to care in the last two years, approximately 1,500 per day

employment_tipping_point.value: Care pressure converts into a graded employment response: schedule reduction, accumulated strain, or exit, rather than a single work-versus-care decision.

observations.period: July 14-17, 2026; workplace impact and strain

denominator.unit: UK adults; employee and current-carer bases vary

workplace_impact_with_caring_experience.unit: percent of employees with caring experience saying caring impacted their workplace

workplace_impact_current_carers.unit: percent of current carers saying caring negatively affected employment

stress_or_tiredness_affecting_work.unit: percent of UK adults; 18% among current carers

no_reported_work_impact_current_carers.unit: percent of current carers saying care did not affect work

support_buffer_mechanism.value: Care does not produce one uniform employment outcome; intensity, duration, employer flexibility, formal care, and other support likely shape whether pressure becomes disruption.

observations.period: September 16, 2026; policy conversion proposed by the report

denominator.unit: UK adults; advocacy recommendations are not survey estimates

paid_carers_leave_proposal.unit: days of paid Carer's Leave called for by Carers UK

leave_conversion.value: The report treats unpaid leave as financially unusable for many carers and frames paid leave plus stronger employment rights as a way to keep care from converting into preventable labour-market exit.

rows.title: Unpaid carers face a durable time-and-work conversion constraint while service involvement remains limited
rows.source_unit: Department of Health and Social Care, Survey of Adult Carers in England 2025 to 2026
rows.geography: England; unpaid adult carers aged 18 and over known to local authorities

observations.period: 2016-17 to 2025-26; carer time, self-care, and social contact

denominator.unit: eligible carers known to English councils in 2025-26; 43,460 responses were received

time_for_value.unit: percent feeling able to spend their time as they want, doing things they value or enjoy

adequate_social_contact.unit: percent saying they have as much social contact as they want with people they like

often_always_lonely.unit: percent reporting often or always feeling lonely

self_care.unit: percent saying they can look after themselves in terms of sleep or eating well

mechanism.value: Unpaid care converts household and public-service gaps into lost discretionary time, constrained social contact, and reduced self-maintenance

observations.period: 2016-17 to 2025-26; work, financial difficulty, and high-intensity care

denominator.unit: eligible carers known to English councils in 2025-26; employment and caring measures are response distributions within that survey

not_in_paid_work_due_to_care.unit: percent saying they are not in paid employment because of caring responsibilities

a_lot_financial_difficulty.unit: percent saying caring caused them a lot of financial difficulties in the last 12 months

care_100_plus_hours.unit: percent spending 100 or more hours per week looking after or helping the person they care for

health_effects.value: 79.4% felt tired, 67.1% reported disturbed sleep, and 64.8% reported general stress

mechanism.value: High unpaid-care intensity can be converted into employment exit, financial pressure, sleep loss, and stress, making care a household room and labor-market constraint

observations.period: 2023-24 to 2025-26; service satisfaction, involvement, and information access

denominator.unit: eligible carers known to English councils; service-satisfaction figures exclude carers who had not received local-authority support or services

extremely_satisfied_support.unit: percent of carers who received local-authority support or services and were extremely satisfied

always_involved_or_consulted.unit: percent saying they always felt involved or consulted in discussions about support services

easy_information.unit: percent finding information or advice very or fairly easy to find

did_not_try_information.unit: percent who had not tried to find information or advice about support, services, or benefits

mechanism.value: Service contact does not automatically become voice or usable support: involvement, information reach, satisfaction, and substantive care adequacy are separate stages

rows.title: Demographic change is reorganizing labor, care, housing, migration, regional cohesion, and public finance at the same time
rows.source_unit: European Commission Joint Research Centre, Demographic transformation in the EU: challenges and opportunities, July 14, 2026
rows.geography: European Union; population, labor-market, care, housing, migration, and regional-policy synthesis

observations.period: 2024–2100 EU population and longevity projections

denominator.unit: million EU residents at the current population peak cited by the report

population_change.unit: percent projected decline from the current population peak to 2100

life_expectancy_2024.unit: years life expectancy at birth in 2024

mechanism.value: Population decline and longer lives create simultaneous pressure on labor supply, care demand, public finance, housing, and regional continuity rather than a single aging effect

observations.period: 2024–2050 EU age structure and healthy longevity

denominator.unit: EU population projection frame; age shares and life-course indicators

age_65_2050.value: nearly one in three EU residents projected to be age 65 or older by 2050, compared with about one in five today

healthy_life_years.unit: years without major illness expected for a child born in the EU in 2023

care_need_2070.value: people needing support projected to rise from 36 million to 48 million by 2070

mechanism.value: The care economy becomes a central labor, time, health, and public-finance system as longevity increases and the population needing support expands

observations.period: Current EU labor-market and population-pressure indicators

denominator.unit: EU working-age and youth population frame

outside_labor_market.unit: percent of working-age people outside the labor market

gender_employment_gap.unit: percentage-point gender employment gap cited by the report

youth_neet.unit: million young people not in education, employment, or training

skilled_migration.value: skilled migration is already helping address labor shortages while the report also prioritizes upskilling and reskilling people already in the EU

mechanism.value: Demographic pressure is distributed through participation gaps, gendered work, youth transitions, skills, and migration policy rather than solved by one fertility or retirement intervention

observations.period: EU demographic policy response; 2023–2034 policy architecture

denominator.unit: EU Member States receiving coordinated demographic-policy tools

demography_toolbox.value: EU Demography Toolbox adopted in October 2023 and welcomed by all Member States

policy_routes.value: policy responses cover affordable housing, intergenerational fairness, anti-poverty, lifelong skills, care, rural areas, and regions losing working-age population

future_budget.value: the proposed 2028–2034 EU multiannual financial framework includes demographic change as an objective of national and regional partnership plans

mechanism.value: Demography becomes a coordination problem linking housing, care, work, skills, migration, rural development, and intergenerational fairness across policy levels

rows.title: Family caregiving operates as unpaid social infrastructure while shifting health, work, money, and social costs onto caregivers
rows.source_unit: Pew Research Center American Trends Panel survey of US adults with aging parents or spouses/partners

observations.period: September 2-8, 2025; reported in February 2026

denominator.unit: US adults surveyed; 1,193 identify as caregivers for an aging parent, spouse, or partner

parent_caregiver.unit: percent of all US adults identifying as a caregiver for a parent age 65 or older

spouse_partner_caregiver.unit: percent of all US adults identifying as a caregiver for an aging spouse or partner

among_people_with_aging_parent.unit: percent identifying as a caregiver among adults with a parent age 65 or older

among_people_with_aging_spouse.unit: percent identifying as a caregiver among adults with an aging spouse or partner

observations.period: September 2-8, 2025; caregiving tasks and household role

denominator.unit: Pew survey respondents identifying as caregivers for an aging parent, spouse, or partner; task-specific valid universes vary

regular_parent_care_tasks.value: about 68% of parent caregivers regularly help with at least one of errands/housework/home repairs, health-care management, financial management, or personal care

regular_spouse_care_tasks.value: about 66% of spouse/partner caregivers regularly help with at least one of the listed tasks

care_tasks.value: tasks include appointments and medication, bills and budgeting, errands and repairs, and bathing or dressing

observations.period: September 2-8, 2025; reported caregiver effects and inequality

denominator.unit: Pew caregiver subgroups with regular-task and impact responses; item-specific valid denominators

lower_income_caregiving.value: 39% of lower-income adults with an aging parent or partner identify as caregivers, versus 23% of middle-income and 16% of upper-income adults

parent_caregiver_negative_effects.value: parent caregivers report more negative than positive effects on emotional well-being, physical health, job/career, financial situation, and social life, while relationship effects tend more positive

gender_emotional_effect.value: 47% of women versus 30% of men caring for a parent report a negative emotional-well-being impact
gender_emotional_effect.unit: percent among parent caregivers with the relevant response

gender_physical_effect.value: 38% of women versus 26% of men report a negative physical-health impact when caring for a parent
gender_physical_effect.unit: percent among parent caregivers with the relevant response

rows.title: Family caregiving is followed by different labor-market paths for women and men
rows.source_unit: NBER Working Paper 31450; survey responses about family caregiving linked to administrative earnings records
rows.geography: United States family caregivers and matched comparison workers; long-term-care and labor-market trajectories

observations.period: U.S. family caregiving and employment trajectories over a 25-year window around reported caregiving onset; paper issued 2023

denominator.unit: years around reported caregiving-episode start

data_linkage.value: survey responses about family caregiving roles are linked to administrative earnings records

women_trajectory.value: relative to a matched comparison group, family caregiving precedes a drop in both earnings and employment for women

men_trajectory.value: men enter family caregiving after experiencing significant labor-supply disruptions
men_trajectory.unit: caregiving-entry timing and prior labor disruption

gender_difference.value: employment trajectories around caregiving vary significantly by gender

decision_reason: The records offer multiple care/access/work signals, but their periods, populations, denominators, and units are heterogeneous. They cannot be pooled or treated as one trend measure without reconciliation.
